The development of this guideline for the treatment of drug-susceptible tuberculosis was a collaborative effort, endorsed by the European Respiratory Society and the US National Tuberculosis Controllers Association. 2. Representatives from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Canadian Thoracic Society, the International Union Against Tuberculosis and Lung Disease, and the World Health Organization also contributed to the creation of this guideline. 3. This guideline provides detailed recommendations for the clinical and public health management of tuberculosis in both children and adults, specifically in settings where diagnostic tools such as mycobacterial cultures, molecular and phenotypic drug susceptibility tests, and radiographic studies are routinely available. 4. All recommendations were developed following a thorough review of the literature and subsequent discussions by an expert committee, using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) methodology. 5. Due to the public health importance of timely diagnosis and effective management of tuberculosis, empiric multidrug treatment is initiated in nearly all cases where active tuberculosis is suspected. 6. Management decisions are influenced by additional factors such as the presence of comorbidities, disease severity, and the patient’s response to treatment. 7. Specific recommendations are provided regarding case management strategies (including directly observed therapy), regimen and dosing selection for adults and children (daily versus intermittent), treatment of tuberculosis in the context of HIV infection (including the duration of tuberculosis treatment and timing of antiretroviral therapy initiation), and management of extrapulmonary disease (e.g., central nervous system or pericardial involvement). 8. 9. For a comprehensive discussion of tuberculosis management and practice recommendations, refer to the full-text online version of the document. 10. The primary objectives of antituberculosis therapy are to cure the individual patient and to minimize the transmission of Mycobacterium tuberculosis to others. Successful treatment benefits both the patient and the community. 11. The goals of tuberculosis therapy include: (1) rapidly reducing the number of actively growing bacilli to decrease disease severity, prevent death, and halt transmission; (2) eradicating persistent bacilli to achieve a durable cure and prevent relapse after therapy completion; and (3) preventing the development of drug resistance during therapy. 12. The decision to initiate combination chemotherapy for tuberculosis is based on clinical, radiographic, laboratory, patient, and public health factors, with clinical judgment and a high index of suspicion playing critical roles. 13. In patients with a high likelihood of tuberculosis or those seriously ill with a disorder suggestive of tuberculosis, empiric treatment with a four-drug regimen should be promptly initiated, even before the results of acid-fast bacilli smear microscopy, molecular tests, and mycobacterial culture are available. 14. Decades of research, including numerous clinical trials, have consistently demonstrated the necessity of using multiple drugs to achieve treatment objectives, minimize drug toxicity, and maximize the likelihood of treatment completion. 15. The success of drug treatment depends on various factors, and studies have shown an increased risk of relapse in patients with more extensive disease (e.g., cavitation or extensive disease on chest radiograph) or slower response to treatment (e.g., delayed culture conversion at 2–3 months). 16. In low-incidence countries, tuberculosis treatment is often overseen by a government public health agency, with coordination between public and private sectors being essential for optimal treatment organization. 17. Patients are typically assigned a public health case manager who assesses barriers to treatment adherence and collaborates with the patient and healthcare providers to develop an individualized case management plan. 18. 19. Given the prolonged duration of tuberculosis treatment, patient involvement in decision-making regarding treatment supervision and overall care is crucial. 20. International standards emphasize the importance of patient-centered approaches in tuberculosis management. 21. 22. For non-English-speaking patients, professional medical interpreter services are preferred over using family or friends as interpreters. 23. Relevant information should be reinforced at each visit, and additional components of the case management plan may include patient reminders, follow-up on missed appointments, use of incentives, home visits, and integration of tuberculosis care with primary and specialty care. 24. Directly observed therapy (DOT), where a healthcare provider observes the patient taking their medications, remains the standard of practice in many tuberculosis programs due to its benefits in ensuring adherence, early recognition of adverse drug reactions, and addressing treatment complications. 25. While self-administered therapy (SAT) has shown similar outcomes to DOT in some studies, DOT is associated with improved treatment success and increased sputum smear conversion during treatment. 26. Decisions regarding the use of DOT should be made collaboratively with the patient, and DOT can be provided in various settings, including the patient’s home, workplace, or other mutually agreed-upon locations. 27. The preferred treatment regimen for drug-susceptible tuberculosis includes an intensive phase of two months with isoniazid (INH), rifampin (RIF), pyrazinamide (PZA), and ethambutol (EMB), followed by a continuation phase of four months with INH and RIF. 28. EMB can be discontinued once drug susceptibility studies confirm susceptibility to INH and RIF. 29. Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) is recommended for patients at risk of neuropathy, such as those who are pregnant, breastfeeding, HIV-infected, or have diabetes, alcoholism, malnutrition, or chronic renal failure. 30. Daily dosing is preferred for both the intensive and continuation phases of treatment, although five-day-per-week DOT is an acceptable alternative based on clinical experience. 31. Twice-weekly regimens should not be used in HIV-infected patients or those with smear-positive and/or cavitary disease, as missed doses can lead to inferior outcomes. 32. For patients with cavitation on initial chest radiograph and positive cultures at two months of therapy, extending the continuation phase with INH and RIF for an additional three months is recommended to reduce the risk of relapse.
